tip: Turkish greetings take the plural -lar: akşamlar (evenings), not singular akşam. Same pattern shows up in iyi geceler.
Ability comes from -ebilir: dene (try) plus -ebilir gives deneyebilir, and a y slips in between the two vowels.
A specific object takes accusative -i: dilleri means those particular languages, not diller for languages in general.
No word for costs or is: Bilet kırk beş lira states the price directly. Turkish drops the linking verb here.
olsun is the let-it-be form of olmak: kutlu olsun literally means may it be blessed, the way you congratulate.
sonra (after) takes the ablative on the noun: yolculuk becomes yolculuktan, so yolculuktan sonra means after the trip.
Motion toward a place uses dative -e: bahçe becomes bahçeye, meaning to the garden.
Location uses locative -de: ev plus -de gives evde, at home. It answers where something happens.
To show whose, the owner takes -in and the thing takes -i: Öğrencilerin ödevleri means the students' homework.
bit- alone means end by itself; add -ir to give it a doer: bitirdi means he finished it, not just it ended.
For a span of time up to now, add -dir to the amount: iki yıldır means for two years now.
-ınca means when or once: emekli ol plus -unca gives olunca, once I retire. It sets the timing of the next clause.
-muş can mark a realization: unutmuşum means it turns out I forgot, something you notice rather than state flatly.
For will be, Turkish uses olacak (olmak plus future -acak): proje başarılı olacak means the project will be successful.
Obligation uses -malı: yap plus -malı plus -yız gives yapmalıyız, meaning we must prepare.
diye can give a reason: gelecek diye mutluyum means I'm happy that he'll come, marking the thought behind the feeling.
Yepyeni shows adjective intensifying: repeat the first sound of yeni (new) with p to get brand new.
A polite request pairs the aorist with the question word: bakar mısın means could you check, softer than an order.
Turkish puts relative clauses before the noun with -diği: gittiğimiz otel means the hotel we went to.
For in order to, use the -mek verb plus için: göndermek için means in order to send. The verb stays in dictionary form.
gibi means like and follows the noun it compares: pamuk gibi bulutlar means clouds like cotton.
hem... hem frames two qualities together: hem sağlıklı hem ekonomik means both healthy and economical.
For a past habit (used to), add -di to the aorist: temizlerdi means she used to clean, a repeated routine.
-li turns a place into from there: nere plus -li plus -siniz gives Nerelisiniz, where are you from.
The yes/no word harmonizes with the last vowel: after boş (o) it becomes mu, so Bu yer boş mu asks is this seat free.
